title: Asymmetric Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Locally Recoverable Codes
authors: Vijay Kumar, Ramakrishna Bandi
abstract:
arXiv:2610.23889v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Locally recoverable codes (LRCs) permit reconstruction of a lost coordinate from a small subset of the remaining coordinates, a property that is a fundamental coding technique for distributed storage and, more recently, for fault-tolerant quantum memories and distributed storage systems. Existing constructions of quantum locally recoverable codes (qLRCs) and their entanglement-assisted generalizations (EA-qLRCs) impose a single locality parameter $r$ governing recovery from both bit-flip ($X$-type) and phase-flip ($Z$-type) errors, even though physical noise is rarely symmetric between the two. We introduce entanglement-assisted quantum locally recoverable codes (EA-qLRC) with \emph{asymmetric locality} $\{r_X,r_Z\}$, in which $X$-type and $Z$-type errors are corrected from recovery sets of size at most $r_X+1$ and $r_Z+1$, respectively. We extend a stabilizer sufficient condition for this property and, in particular, the CSS framework, where asymmetric locality corresponds to separate locality conditions on the two classical codes $\mathcal C_1$ and $\mathcal C_2$ underlying the construction. From this characterization we derive Singleton-, Griesmer-, Plotkin-, sphere-packing-, and Cadambe\textendash Mazumdar-like bounds for CSS-type asymmetric EA-qLRCs (AEA-qLRCs) built from Proposition~\ref{CSS-EA-qLRC-Asym}, and we characterize exactly when a pure CSS-type AEA-qLRC built from a pair of classical LRCs attains the Singleton-like bound with equality.

title: Transient Heat Conduction on Quantum Hardware: Replicated Temperature-Field Reconstruction and Shot-Count Sensitivity with a Variational Quantum Linear Solver
authors: Yijin Mao, Yuwen Zhang
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24004v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Implicit discretizations of transient heat conduction repeatedly generate sparse linear systems, making diffusion problems a natural test bed for quantum linear solvers. This study evaluates how accurately a variational quantum linear solver (VQLS) recovers the temperature field produced by one backward-Euler step of one-dimensional conduction on IBM quantum hardware. A pre-specified confirmatory experiment compares N=4 interior temperatures encoded on two qubits with N=8 temperatures encoded on three qubits using ten paired hardware blocks; a separately defined N=16, four-qubit extension is evaluated in five independently scheduled exploratory blocks. Local VQLS optimization reduces relative temperature-field error to approximately 10^{-8} for all three cases, establishing an essentially exact ideal reference at this scale. On hardware, mean relative L2 temperature-field error is 8.07% for N=4 and 20.14% for N=8, a paired increase of 12.06 percentage points (95% CI, 10.71-13.42; exact paired sign-flip p=0.001953). The exploratory N=16 mean is 24.75+/-1.84%. A pre-specified N=16 shot-count follow-up then evaluates the same locked circuit at 2,048, 8,192, and 32,768 shots in six independently scheduled blocks. Mean field error remains 23.64%, 24.57%, and 24.37%, respectively; the 32,768-minus-2,048-shot contrast is +0.74 percentage points (95% CI, -0.65 to 2.12; p=0.281). In contrast, ideal multinomial sampling predicts a reduction from 2.68% to 0.75%. Higher shot counts reduce block-to-block variability but do not recover the mean cold-side temperature field. The results show that full-field readout of a strongly nonuniform thermal state is limited by more than ordinary finite-shot sampling under the tested hardware conditions, motivating observable-focused quantum formulations for heat flux, stored energy, and selected temperatures.

title: Designing Robust Quantum Gates
authors: Yuanxing Hao, Marin Bukov
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24039v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: For given control channels, quantum control theory determines whether quantum gates can be realized, but not their resilience to errors. We address this problem by establishing existence criteria for robust gate implementation in $d$-level systems. Our criteria reveal that implementability of all gates is not enough: a universal family of robust gates exists if and only if the driven Hamiltonians share no common symmetry. When these criteria hold, we can make gates resilient to any combination of static perturbations, uniform Hamiltonian rescaling, perturbations at a finite set of selected frequencies, and perturbations with arbitrary selected waveforms. We can impose robustness conditions broadly with limited information about errors, e.g., against any static perturbations; we can also tailor these conditions to the platform, e.g., against environment-induced noise with dominant spectral peaks, requiring no spectral details beyond the peak frequencies. We numerically construct explicit protocols for robust gates, reducing average gate infidelity by approximately two to seven orders of magnitude under Hamiltonian perturbations and environment-induced noise. Together, our existence criteria and numerical constructions provide practical guidance for evaluating the potential of quantum platforms and designing robust quantum gates.

title: Residual Carleman lift for nonlinear lattice Boltzmann simulations
authors: Ilya Karlin
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24041v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Low-order Carleman embeddings replace nonlinear dynamics by a larger linear system, but truncation errors can accumulate even when the underlying nonlinear model is accurately approximated by a quadratic equation. We construct a residual Carleman lift (RC2) of lattice Boltzmann dynamics in which an independently evolved spectral background supplies the coefficients and forcing of a second-order residual lift. In a double-shear-layer test, conventional fixed-rest Carleman reaches $87.3\%$ final error, whereas prepared RC2 achieves $0.136\%$ through vortex roll-up, without restarting the lift or using fine-reference feedback. The results demonstrate control of the finite-time accuracy of a fixed-order linear embedding through nonlinear preparation.

title: Operational Meaning of the Mandelstam-Tamm Time Scale in a Spin-1/2 Clock
authors: Jakub (James),  Rog
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24056v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Georgiev's analysis of a freely precessing spin correctly emphasizes that the Mandelstam-Tamm quantity $\Delta T=\Delta\hat A/|d\langle\hat A\rangle/d t|$ is not the variance of a time operator. He concludes, however, that its divergence near the extrema of the clock signal is devoid of physical meaning and that $\Delta T$ does not disclose how well the system measures the passage of time. For the same projective $\hat\sigma_x$ readout, we show that $\Delta T$ equals the inverse square root of the classical Fisher information in one binary outcome at regular operating points. Its divergence at submaximal-coherence extrema therefore identifies a loss of local sensitivity in the selected readout, not an infinite variance of physical time; a complementary $\hat\sigma_y$ measurement remains informative. This interpretation also separates Georgiev's exactly known tick--tock period from the statistical precision with which a tick can be located. It preserves his warning against a time-operator interpretation while qualifying his stronger conclusion that the Mandelstam--Tamm scale lacks physical content.

title: Quantum error correction well below the color code threshold
authors: Ali Lavasani, Adam P. Reed, Joan M. Dreiling, Annie J. Park, Michael Mills, Matteo Puviani, Gabriel Matos, M. S. Allman, Noah Berthusen, Natalie C. Brown, Victor E. Colussi, Brian Estey, Cameron Foltz, Daniel Gresh, Reza Haghshenas, Akhil Isanaka, Nikhil Kotibhaskar, Anthony Ransford, Ciar\'an Ryan-Anderson, Brian Neyenhuis, David Hayes, Tzvetan S. Metodi, Andrew C. Potter
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24077v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum error correction enables scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation by suppressing logical errors exponentially with code distance once physical error rates fall below a critical threshold. Here we demonstrate below-threshold operation of triangular color codes with distances $d=3,5,$ and $7$ on Quantinuum's Helios trapped-ion quantum processor. Leveraging both circuit- and hardware- level leakage reduction schemes, we achieve logical error rates as low as $5_{-2}^{+4}\times 10^{-6}$, and demonstrate error suppression by over an order of magnitude, $\Lambda=12_{-2}^{+3}$, with each successive increase in code distance. Moreover, we demonstrate below threshold scaling of error rates for Clifford two-qubit randomized benchmarking circuits when encoded in $d=3,5$ color codes, achieving logical error rate of $7^{+3}_{-3}\times 10^{-5}$ per logical two-qubit Clifford at distance $5$ with a suppression factor of $\Lambda=9_{-3}^{+8}$. We compare logical performance for existing near-optimal algorithmic decoders, and both convolutional neural network and transformer-based neural network decoders capable of real-time decoding an order of magnitude faster than the syndrome extraction rate. These results approach the logical error rates required for megaquop-scale quantum computation and indicate that scaled trapped-ion processors could reach application-relevant performance with substantially smaller code blocks than indicated by previous results in other qubit modalities.

title: Performance of a Hot Rb Vapour-Based Portable Quantum Memory
authors: Kenneth Gregory, Konrad Socha, Khaled Mnaymneh, Connor Kupchak
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24098v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum repeaters will be paramount to the success of the future quantum internet. Presently however, the losses incurred in fibre communications are unsustainable when fragile quantum states are transmitted over long distances. The most effective repeater nodes will require incorporation of a minimum of two quantum memory units (QMems) for successful operation. Therefore a network composed of numerous nodes will ideally require scalable repeaters that contain QMems that are portable, robust and do not require a high amount of overhead. Here we investigate the performance of a commercial QMem based on a warm vapour of Rb atoms. Specifically, we characterize the coherence time, absolute efficiency, signal to noise ratio and bit error ratio of this device over a range of vapour temperatures that are readily controllable. For our system, we place these performance metrics into the same conventions as those established for current optical communication protocols. Development of QMem systems meeting these benchmarks will be a vital step for seamless integration of QMems systems into present-day communication architectures.

title: From Critical Transitions to Sustainability Transformations: Phenomena, Theory, and Applications Across Disciplines
authors: Elisabeth H. Krueger, Koustav Halder, Woi Oh, Nusrat Molla, Juan C. Rocha, Giuseppe Ferro, Guillaume Falmagne, Annie B. Stephenson, Lan Wang Erlandsson, Jacques Bara, George I. Hagstrom, Nico Wunderling, Jiayu Li, Xander Huggins, Emma R. Zajdela, Harman Jaggi, Sara M. Constantino, Caronline Schill, Vitor V. Vasconcelos
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24119v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: There has been a recent surge in the use of terms describing systemic change processes across science, policy, and public debate. The associated change phenomena are often assumed to be abrupt and irreversible once critical thresholds are crossed. However, the interchangeable use of terms leaves definitions and the underpinning scientific theory unclear, which can lead to misconceptions about transition processes and potential impacts. Here, we present selected empirical examples representing phenomena of tipping points, regime shifts, critical transitions, phase transitions, social and socio-technical transitions, and sustainability transformations, together with their underlying theory derived from the broadly defined domains of physics and mathematics, Earth science and ecology, social sciences, and their interdisciplinary overlaps. We bring these fields into closer conversation, creating a shared understanding of each of the conceptual roots, phenomena, mechanisms, and specific applications. This can help steward the governance of social-ecological change towards more just and sustainable futures.

title: Translation-Invariant Pure States with Exotic Half-Chain Factors
authors: Ruizhi Liu, Jinmin Yi
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24154v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We construct translation-invariant pure quasifree fermionic states on the one-dimensional lattice whose half-chain von Neumann algebras are hyperfinite factors of type $\mathrm{II}_\infty$ or $\mathrm{III}_\lambda$ for any $0<\lambda\leq 1$. Via the Jordan-Wigner-Araki transformation, these yield translation-invariant pure spin-chain states with the same half-chain factors, demonstrating that such factors need not be of type I or III. Each state is the unique ground state of a gapless, translation-invariant parent Hamiltonian with superpolynomially decaying interactions. For any fixed factor type, the interval entanglement entropy can exhibit widely varying growth rates, from arbitrarily slow divergence to nearly power-law growth, showing that entropy scaling does not determine the factor type. In contrast, we prove that gauge-invariant quadratic Hamiltonians with finitely many flavours and exponentially decaying hopping exhibit a dichotomy: their ground states either satisfy an area law with a type I half-chain factor, or have logarithmic entropy growth with a type $\mathrm{III}_1$ factor. The counterexample was discovered with AI assistance.

title: Trajectree - A quantum trajectory-based quantum circuit simulator
authors: Ansh Singal, Allen Zang, Jordan Thomas, Alexander Kolar, Anirudh Ramesh, Joaquin Chung, Rajkumar Kettimuthu, Prem Kumar
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24160v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce Trajectree, a quantum trajectory-based quantum circuit simulator that uses a novel, state-saving partial execution of the quantum circuits to simulate broad and deep noisy quantum circuits efficiently. Trajectree can efficiently generate a large number of Monte Carlo samples by saving partially executed trajectories. We conduct extensive performance analysis of the Trajectree approach, proving the utility of the trajectory saving scheme for simulations of open quantum systems. Using this architecture, we show that Trajectree can simulate standard benchmark noisy circuits over five times faster than Google's QSim, a part of the Cirq package. We also analyze Trajectree's performance for simulating quantum optical systems relevant to communication and computing applications. We demonstrate applications of the optical backend to simulate three optical experiments: CHSH Bell test, entanglement swapping, and optical CNOT gate. This shows Trajectree's potential for simulating noisy qudit and optical systems efficiently.

title: Probing wetting and solidification dynamics of neon thin films with a high-$T_c$ superconducting circuit
authors: Brennan Dizdar, Yueheng Shi, David I. Schuster, Christopher S. Lang
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24167v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Integrating condensed noble gases with superconducting circuits offers new opportunities for operating hybrid quantum devices. In particular, electrons on solid neon have recently emerged as exceptionally coherent charge qubits, however the growth of the underlying neon films on patterned devices remains poorly controlled. We monitor neon films near the triple point using a multimode resonator fabricated from high-$T_c$ YBCO, which remains superconducting at temperatures where the liquid phase exists and whose geometry sets a thickness-sensing window near 1 $\mu$m. In the liquid state we observe rich film dynamics: uniform wetting that saturates near 20 nm, drainage of thicker films, and spontaneous thickness oscillations, reflecting the extreme sensitivity of thick films in this regime. A galvanic connection to our sensing volume enables in-situ electrostatic tuning of the liquid film thickness. Statistics of freezing the neon across various liquid levels reveal variations of the solid film thickness by approximately an order of magnitude. We also observe a two-fold increase in the quality factor of the resonators at the level of $10^3$ with added neon and rule out dielectric loss as the limiting factor. Our results demonstrate that hermetic packaging facilitates the investigation of both rich non-equilibrium fluid dynamics and the impact of condensed noble gas films on microwave loss in superconducting circuits, but may not be the best modality for growing solid neon films with precisely controlled thickness.

title: T-embeddings as stationary measures on T-graphs
authors: Mikhail Basok, Benoit Laslier, Marianna Russkikh
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24180v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this paper, we investigate the relation between t-embeddings and T-graphs associated with the same weighted planar bipartite graph. We prove that, given such a T-graph, the corresponding t-embeddings are classified by positive stationary measures on this T-graph and describe a reconstruction procedure of the t-embedding given such a measure. As an application, we develop an approach for constructing t-embeddings of arbitrary sufficiently non-degenerate planar bipartite graphs.

title: Nonlocality as a Benchmarking Tool for Quantum Processors
authors: Andr\'es Camilo Granda Arango, Carla Sophie Rieger, Carlo Cuccu, Giuseppe Sergioli, Luigi Iapichino, Tobias Valentin Bauer, Roberto Giuntini, Federico Hern\'an Holik
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24196v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Benchmarking quantum processors is a central task in every roadmap aimed at quantum advantage. Here, we discuss a benchmarking protocol based on the violation of the Svetlichny inequality, which is designed to simulate genuine multipartite nonlocality. We compare it with Mermin's inequality, and present the results of applying this framework to two different quantum processing units -the superconducting system Garnet (from IQM) and the ion-trap system Marmot (from AQT), testing different families of quantum circuits for three to five qubits under identical experimental conditions. We also run simultaneous triplet tests across the full register, including a comparison between GHZ and linear cluster states, to probe how Svetlichny-inequality violations depend on qubit location and calibration. Our results demonstrate that tests based on genuine multipartite nonlocality provide a powerful tool to characterize the collective performance of quantum devices and to guide their calibration and optimization.

title: Optimal robust single-qubit gates in superconducting quantum processors
authors: Tangyou Huang, Anuj Aggarwal, Jingjun Zhu, Akshay Gaikwad, David Niepce, Marcus Rommel, Andreas Nylander, Amr Osman, Anita Fadavi Rousari, Janka Bizn\'arov\'a, St\'ephane Gu\'erin, Gheorghe Sorin Paraoanu, Anton Frisk Kockum, Giovanna Tancredi
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24212v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires high-fidelity quantum gates that are resilient to control errors and device imperfections. Here, we develop energy-optimal control pulses for single-qubit gates that are simultaneously robust against frequency detuning and waveform inhomogeneities while also suppressing leakage outside the computational subspace. Combining the optimized pulse envelopes with an adaptive control scheme, we experimentally demonstrate optimal robust gates on a superconducting quantum processor. For a gate duration of 90ns, we achieve fidelities above 99.9% for the X gate and 99.6% for Hadamard-type gates. For the X gate, we maintain fidelities above 99.5% for simultaneous drive-amplitude variations up to 20% and qubit detuning up to 4 MHz. This robustness outperforms that of conventional Gaussian pulses by an order of magnitude, without much difference in peak gate fidelity. These results establish a route towards robust single-qubit control in large-scale quantum processors, advancing the development of fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Generalized Svetlichny Inequalities as a Cross-Platform Benchmark for Quantum Processors
authors: Andr\'es Camilo Granda Arango, Giuseppe Sergioli, Luigi Iapichino, Tobias Valentin Bauer, Carlo Cuccu, Roberto Giuntini
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24213v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A cross-platform benchmark should be device-independent yet sensitive to imperfections accumulated during execution. Building on prior work, we formulate and validate a protocol through demonstrations based on generalized Svetlichny inequality violations (a simulation, rather than a loophole-free certification, of multipartite nonlocality) for larger subsystem sizes. We apply it unchanged to three processors, the trapped-ion Marmot and IBEX Q1 (both manufactured by AQT) and the superconducting Euro-Q-Exa System 1 (IQM), using identical GHZ-state circuits with fixed theoretical measurement settings from N=2 to N=10 qubits. Both trapped-ion processors sustain violations up to ten qubits, while the superconducting processor loses them beyond six qubits under unmitigated (raw) conditions; readout-error mitigation recovers violations up to eight qubits, with a substantial fraction of the degradation attributable to measurement imperfections. These processors provide a heterogeneous testbed for validating the protocol's cross-platform applicability and discriminating power, demonstrating its practicality as a common framework for assessing collective quantum performance.

title: A large nonmagnetic aluminum-and-Viton vacuum chamber suitable for vacuum pressures down into the extremely-high-vacuum (XHV) regime
authors: N. T. McCall, H. -M. Yau, Z. Corriveau, J. Perez Garcia, T. Chauhan, G. K. Koyanagi, R. L. Lambo, M. C. George, C. H. Storry, E. A. Hessels
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24262v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A recently constructed large nonmagnetic vacuum chamber is described and characterized. The vacuum chamber was machined from 19-inch cubes of aluminum and are sealed using dual Viton O-rings (with the interspace between the O-rings evacuated by a separate vacuum pump). 17-inch-diameter openings on all six sides allow for easy access to the experimental apparatus and for vacuum pumps with very large pumping speeds. These 17-inch holes were bored straight through the aluminum cube, resulting in an interior volume of 100 L (almost 90\% of the total volume of the 19-inch cube). The 17-inch openings are sealed with 19-inch-diameter aluminum flanges. The system is modular in that the cubes can be connected to one another to form larger vacuum systems. The chamber is designed to allow for vacuum pressures of $10^{-12}$ torr. In many respects (including nonmagnetic properties, outgassing rate after low-temperature baking, weight, cost, ease of machining, and ease of baking due to the chamber's high thermal conductivity) this system is superior to standard stainless-steel metal-sealed CF vacuum systems and is highly recommended for use by others.

title: Encoding Hyperuniformity in Geometric Networks: Structural Signatures and Diffusion Dynamics
authors: Yongyi Wang, Eli Newby, Yang Jiao, Salvatore Torquato, R\'eka Albert
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24317v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Disordered hyperuniformity is a recently discovered exotic state exhibiting anomalously suppressed density fluctuations at long wavelengths, and its generalization to network systems remains an important open question. Here, we show that, across a wide range of systems, geometric networks retain substantially more long-wavelength density information from the underlying point configurations than Delaunay triangulations. Within geometric networks, hyperuniformity manifests as suppressed vertex-to-vertex fluctuations in a range of network structural observables, including closeness centrality, vertex strength, and eigenvector centrality. These measures not only distinguish hyperuniform networks from non-hyperuniform ones, but also separate near-hyperuniform configurations from hyperuniform systems with strong local disorder, solving a central challenge in network hyperuniformity. We connect these structural signatures to network dynamics by introducing a relaxation-time centrality based on diffusion and demonstrate that hyperuniform geometric networks exhibit more homogeneous relaxation behavior than non-hyperuniform geometric networks. These results reveal how the suppression of large-scale density fluctuations manifests in both network structure and diffusion dynamics.

title: Microcomb spectral fingerprinting enables parts-per-trillion methane detection with low humidity cross-sensitivity
authors: Shiyan Cao, Yinchao Xu, Judith Su
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24338v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Optical frequency combs have transformed molecular spectroscopy by enabling broadband, high-resolution analysis, yet they are conventionally used as light sources to interrogate external samples. Here, we introduce an integrated microcomb sensing architecture that unifies resonantly enhanced evanescent sensing with multiwavelength molecular fingerprinting in a single ultrahigh-quality-factor silica microresonator. Gaseous analytes interact directly with the evanescent field of light recirculating within the resonator, enhancing sensitivity while encoding analyte-induced perturbations across the microcomb's collective spectral response. Rather than relying on a single optical resonance, we exploit distributed responses across multiple comb lines to generate multidimensional molecular fingerprints. Adding more comb lines systematically improves analyte discrimination, showing that the microcomb provides sensing information beyond what individual spectral channels offer. Using methane as a model analyte, we achieve an estimated detection limit of 178 parts per trillion, with minimal spectral responses to ammonia, carbon monoxide, hexane, and water vapor at relative humidities up to 90%. By replacing physically long interaction paths with resonant light recirculation in an ultrahigh-Q microresonator, this architecture brings compact optical sensing into the parts-per-trillion regime while exploiting distributed spectral information for chemical identification.

title: Maximum-Temperature Theorem for a Nanothermometer
authors: Taras Plakhotnik
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24340v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The steady-state temperature predicted for an ideal point heat source diverges in conventional heat-conduction theory, but no physical thermometer measures a point value. We derive a sharp, shape-independent upper bound on the quasi-steady temperature rise of a sensor with thermometric volume $V_\mathrm{s}$, placed anywhere inside a region enclosed by an isothermal reference surface. The bound requires only the total heat power generated in the region $\dot{Q}$, a lower bound on its thermal conductivity $\kappa_\mathrm{m}$, and the value of $V_\mathrm{s}$. It is otherwise independent of the heat-source distribution, domain shape, and source--sensor distance. For $\dot{Q}=50~\mathrm{pW}$, $\kappa_\mathrm{m} = 0.1~\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $V_\mathrm{s}=10^{-22}\mathrm{\,m^3}$, approximately the volume of a $60~\mathrm{nm}$-diameter sphere, the theorem permits a maximum temperature rise of approximately $2~\mathrm{mK}$ above the reference level. The result applies directly to nanodiamonds, upconversion nanoparticles, fluorescent polymer particles, and core-shell quantum dots. It shows that neither source localization nor uncertain source-sensor separation can account for kelvin-scale readings under steady-state heat conduction.

title: Quantum-Classical Iterative Refinement for the Pressure-Poisson Equation on NISQ Hardware
authors: Doyeol "David" Ahn (Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Seoul, Seoul, Republic of Korea 2 Singularity Quantum Inc., Newport Beach, CA, USA 3 Center for Quantum Information Processing, University of Seoul, Seoul, Republic of Korea 4 School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Gyeongsang National University, Jinju, Republic of Korea 5 National Quantum Laboratory at Maryland), Byeongyong Park, Rho Shin Myong, Franz Klein
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24342v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present a hybrid quantum-classical iterative refinement for the pressure-Poisson equation of the incompressible Navier-Stokes projection method on noisy quantum hardware. Rather than solving the pressure equation once per time step, we solve it repeatedly for the normalized residual and scale each quantum direction by a least-squares fit to the physical residual. As a result, the error of the quantum solve enters as a contraction factor $\sin\theta_k$ of the residual rather than as an error floor. This removes the requirement of a state infidelity below $10^{-7}$ that was estimated for single-solve schemes. With a boundary-consistent staggered (MAC) discretization, the pressure residual equals the velocity divergence left after projection up to the factor $\Delta t/\rho$. On the IBM processor ibm_cleveland, a four-qubit ($16\times16$) problem reached a relative residual below $10^{-7}$ within eight to ten corrections in all 20 runs of a pre-registered experiment, whereas a single solve with a comparable number of shots stopped at 0.33-0.59. In a six-qubit ($64\times64$) pilot, all three runs reached the same tolerance in 13 corrections. On the IonQ Forte processor, a manufactured-solution benchmark reached $5.6\times10^{-8}$ in nine corrections, with a pressure error of $4.9\times10^{-8}$. Finally, we carried out the variational training itself on ibm_cleveland, so that every sampled value of the cost function was obtained from hardware measurements. The residual fell to $5.6\times10^{-4}$ in seven corrections, below the pre-specified tolerance of $10^{-3}$, at the rate predicted by a noise model and with 24 min of QPU time.

title: FTWeave: Composing Logical Execution, Real-Time Decoding, and Magic-State Supply in Tightly Integrated Quantum-Classical Systems
authors: Panayiotis Christou, Shuwen Kan, Ying Mao
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24344v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum applications depend on both decoded measurement information and a continuing supply of magic states. While an operation waits for either, its logical data require protection that produces more syndrome data and decoding work. Architects must provision the quantum and classical parts of the machine together, before complete systems are available to measure. FTWeave is a system-level simulator for this architectural exploration. It accepts OpenQASM 2/3 circuits, CUDA-Q Logical compiler artifacts, Stim circuits, and provider-derived physical inputs through adapters that preserve operation and measurement dependencies. Users bind these inputs to quantum resources, classical processors, memory, communication, and factory configurations. One event timeline determines application progress, resource ownership, and continuing protection. This supplies the system model needed to connect circuit and decoder evidence to application performance. Controlled demand studies and complete multiplier and Ising circuits show why the coupling changes provisioning decisions. A fixed-work approximation predicts a 3.55x multiplier speedup from additional factories where the coupled model gives almost none. Explicit ownership also changes useful capacity: increasing decoder workers alone has no benefit in a storage-constrained case, while increasing workers and feedback entries together gives 4.93x speedup. Selected color and hypergraph-product code mappings take 53-90% longer under decoder service variability, despite an unchanged mean. These comparisons identify useful resource combinations and distinguish protection work from the elapsed lifetime of quantum data.

title: EntangledEdge: A Distributed System for Orbital Quantum Sensing and Learning
authors: Mohammad Abrarul Hasanat, Amit Samanta, Jason Ludmir, Tirthak Patel, Rohan Basu Roy
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24353v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An orbital quantum sensor is more precise than classical and holds its information in a quantum state's superposition and entanglement, which classical measurement collapses. Learning on quantum-sensed data therefore requires a distributed system in which the data stay quantum from sensor to inference. We present EntangledEdge, the first system architecture to unify orbital quantum sensing and learning end-to-end, with a quantum data plane and a classical control plane. It routes each event to a channel-matched model in a capacity-diverse bank, adapts its detection threshold without labels, and aggregates across stations by hardware fidelity. Evaluated with a hybrid prototype (real quantum processors, simulated orbit-to-ground link) over satellite telemetry, EntangledEdge achieves high-quality inference at bounded per-event cost, improves quantum processor utilization, and scales with fleet size.

title: Hidden urban exposure to energy-price shocks: spreading burdens and shifting hotspots
authors: Yunfei Bai, Aaron Tesfa Tsion, Ra\'ul Rosales, Barbara Shollock, Wei He
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24388v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cities need to anticipate where energy-price shocks could intensify hardship beyond established hotspots. How income distributions and fuel-price balances jointly shape this hidden exposure remains unclear. Here we address this gap by stress-testing nearly one million properties in six English local authorities, combining required-energy costs for existing housing with modelled local income distributions. Under gas-led crisis prices, 41% of neighbourhoods in the highest local exposure quarter lie outside the highest official fuel-poverty quarter. Electricity-led stress changes this hidden geography: when electricity unit prices alone triple from 2021, comparable to the unmitigated late-2022 cap increase, 38% of the resulting hidden-exposure group are absent from the crisis-based group. Entering neighbourhoods have newer, more efficient housing, more flats and greater electricity dependence than retained areas. Crisis preparedness should extend household protection beyond current hardship hotspots, using fuel-specific stress tests to anticipate support needs as fuel prices and heating systems change.

title: Freeform gradient-index media reconstruction
authors: V. Ch\'{a}vez-Islas, F. H. Maldonado-Villamizar, E. Esp\'{i}ndola-Ramos, S. Ch\'{a}vez-Cerda, J. E. G\'{o}mez-Correa
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24393v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reconstructing a gradient-index (GRIN) medium consists of determining a spatial refractive index distribution that produces a prescribed ray trajectory, an inverse problem in geometrical optics. Previous approaches have used geometrical symmetries and conserved ray quantities to address this inverse problem. Extending reconstruction to freeform media requires approaches that do not rely on these symmetries. Here, we present a three-dimensional point-wise method for reconstructing freeform GRIN media through the inverse application of local refraction. The method does not require geometrical symmetry, paraxial approximations, or prior knowledge of the iso-indicial surfaces, and is straightforward to implement. Reconstruction using two interface geometries demonstrates that different refractive index distributions can be obtained from the same prescribed trajectory function. The choice of interfaces thus provides an additional degree of freedom for optical design, subject to local refraction conditions and compatibility between overlapping reconstructed regions.

title: Prototype-Guided Optimization of Quantum Data Embeddings with Linear Cost
authors: Seokhoon Jeong, Daniel K. Park
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24403v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In supervised quantum machine learning with classical data, classification performance critically depends on the geometry induced by quantum data embedding. Existing data-adaptive approaches rely on pairwise fidelity evaluations between samples, which scale as $O(B^2)$ for $B$ samples and create a computational bottleneck in iterative embedding optimization. To address this issue, we propose a prototype-guided framework for efficient data-adaptive quantum embedding. Using class-prototype separation and sample-to-prototype compactness, we derive a measurable lower certificate for class-ensemble distinguishability and construct a prototype-based objective requiring only $O(B)$ fidelity evaluations. We integrate this objective into an end-to-end pipeline that combines task-specific quantum circuit architecture optimization with continuous refinement of the data-embedding parameters. Across five benchmark datasets with up to 20 qubits, our method retains competitive quantum kernel support vector machine (SVM) performance while reducing fidelity-evaluation cost, with particularly strong gains over budget-matched pairwise optimization on T-MNIST. Geometric analyses examine how the learned embeddings relate to kernel alignment and classification margins, revealing dataset-dependent benefits and limitations. We further derive a prototype-based classifier in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space that provides an explicit witness for the SVM objective and a low-cost proxy for model selection, and extend the framework to multiple prototypes for multimodal class structures.

title: Margin-Based Generalization for Quantum Machine Learning with Classical Data Encoding
authors: Ju-Young Ryu, Tak Hur, Daniel K. Park
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24426v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding generalization is essential for assessing the practical viability of quantum machine learning. In many applications, quantum models operate on classical data that must first be encoded into quantum states, making the encoding part of the effective hypothesis class. We develop a margin-based generalization framework for this setting, covering both fixed and trainable quantum data encodings. For fixed encodings, the existing margin bound transfers unchanged. For trainable encodings, we derive a bound using a two-scale covering argument that combines the original margin-dependent term with an additive encoding-capacity term of order $\tilde O(\sqrt{L/m})$, where $L$ is the number of trainable encoding parameters and $m$ is the training-sample size. Across 19,440 simulated training runs spanning various image datasets, circuit architectures, and optimization settings, the inverse margin performs best among five baseline and two bound-derived complexity measures under conditional-independence and 90th-percentile sign-error criteria, within bootstrap uncertainty. These results provide a unified margin-based view of generalization in quantum machine learning with classical data.

title: Beyond low-dissipation regime: general condition for Curzon-Ahlborn efficiency
authors: Yuki Izumida
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24434v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In recent years, physicists have extensively investigated the universality of Curzon-Ahlborn (CA) efficiency as the efficiency at maximum power of heat engines, which, like Carnot efficiency, is determined only by heat-bath temperatures. While the universality of the CA efficiency to the first order in the temperature difference is established within linear response theory in the inverse operation time, it is generally lost at quadratic order. In the low-dissipation Carnot heat engine model known as the standard framework, the symmetric dissipation condition is necessary. Yet, it is not a necessary condition as the original CA model that adopts endoreversibility does not require such symmetry. In this study, we extend the low-dissipation model to include nonlinear response in the inverse operation time and derive a general condition under which the CA efficiency is recovered in the quadratic order. The generalized symmetric dissipation condition and the CA model with Newton's law of cooling are shown to be special cases of this condition. By applying the obtained condition, we also clarify the condition under which an endoreversible model with a general heat-transfer law exhibits the CA efficiency.

title: Energy-optimal scheduling for clocked reversible computing
authors: Michael C. Thumann, David Soloveichik
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24435v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Computational dissipation may arise from both information erasure and finite-time operation, although both contributions can in principle be avoided in the absence of space and time constraints. Logically reversible computation can replace erasure with ancilla cleanup, and slow adiabatic protocols can eliminate any excess finite-time dissipation. Under limited memory and in finite time, however, choosing reversible cleanup over erasure requires additional dissipative operations, creating a semi-reversible energy--memory--time tradeoff. We formulate this tradeoff at a fixed operating point of an externally clocked thermally coupled computer, where reversible checkpoint moves and local irreversible erasures have specified effective prices $\epsilon_R$ and $\epsilon_I$. Their ratio $\lambda=\epsilon_I/\epsilon_R$ selects an energy-optimal semi-reversible schedule under a checkpoint-memory bound by trading reversible moves against erasures. For a sequential computation whose dependency graph is a line, we derive an exact separator recurrence and prove that an asymptotically optimal schedule repeats a strictly reversible block followed by one local erasure. Coupling this scheduling theorem to a stochastic-thermodynamic constitutive model shows how temperature, primitive duration, memory, and device-dependent operation costs determine whether the optimal schedule uses reversible cleanup, elective erasures, or erasure at every disposal.

title: Certifying Nonlocal Spin Quantum Entanglement from Local Tunneling Spectra
authors: Payman Kazemikhah, Ruolun Zhang, Xiangyu Luo, Byunghoon Kim, Yu-Peng Zhu, Md. Shafayat Hossain, M. Zahid Hasan
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24440v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum entanglement is intrinsically nonlocal, whereas tunneling spectroscopy measures one site at a time. We show that this apparent mismatch can be overcome: local tunneling spectra can certify spin entanglement without coherent control or absolute intensity calibration. An exact spin sum rule turns the high-bias conductance into an internal normalization, allowing the inelastic spin-flip weight to place a lower bound on the local quantum Fisher information. Total-spin conservation then fixes the otherwise inaccessible intersite fluctuation, converting two local spectra into a bound on a collective entanglement witness. We incorporate coupling to the substrate through a spectroscopic bound on spin leakage, while a hierarchy of thresholds distinguishes entanglement between the spins from entanglement with their environment. Including instrumental broadening and noise, the resulting certificate holds at a stated confidence level. These results establish a route for extracting nonlocal quantum information from equilibrium local spectroscopy.

title: Quantum-Correlation-Based Multi-Emitter Localization in Information-Limited Regimes via Learned Inference
authors: Sanket K. Tripathy, Simeon I. Bogdanov
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24457v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum correlation measurements have emerged as a powerful tool for localizing multiple emitters with subwavelength separation. Multi-emitter localization consists of two distinct tasks: identifying the emitter count $N$ and estimating their positions $\left\{x^{i}\right\}$. Existing fit-and-select frameworks fit the measured intensity and autocorrelation data using several models corresponding to different values of $N$ and then select the best-supported model. This procedure lets errors from the multi-parameter optimization of emitter positions propagate into the choice of model, degrading performance under photon-limited and high-background conditions. We propose a method that directly infers the emitter count and positions from the multimodal data via learned inference. Learned inference improves both the emitter-counting accuracy and localization precision compared to the fit-and-select method. It achieves more than tenfold improvement in precision and requires up to five times fewer photons to achieve practically meaningful localization with the largest gains observed under low photon counts, strong background, narrowly spaced emitter configurations, and spatially truncated data. This photon-efficient quantum-assisted localization framework offers a promising route toward real-time biological imaging and single-particle tracking in densely labeled samples.

title: Local response theory of multiparameter sudden-quench quantum Otto engines
authors: Dehua Liu, Yihang Cai, Biao Xiong, Jibing Liu, Chuanjia Shan, Jianhui Wang
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24482v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multiparameter quantum Otto engines raise an optimization problem absent in single-parameter cycles: which small quench vector maximizes the quadratic approximation to the exact output work in a multidimensional control space? We develop a local response theory for sudden-quench Otto engines with quantum working media described by linearly controlled Hamiltonians. We show that the local quadratic work decomposes into a thermal-bias gain and a quadratic response cost, whose competition determines the quench vector that maximizes the local quadratic work at a prescribed quench amplitude. We illustrate the theory in a minimal two-level working medium, where radial and transverse quenches play distinct roles, and in a finite interacting XYZ spin chain, where the resulting quench vector is determined by the balance between thermal-bias and response cost. Our results provide a practical local criterion for designing small multiparameter quenches in sudden-quench quantum Otto engines.

title: Logical-Space Theory of Ordered-Statistics Decoding for Quantum LDPC Codes
authors: Yun Shang
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24503v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum decoding succeeds when a correction matches the logical class of the error, whereas ordered-statistics decoding (OSD) searches a finite list of physical corrections. We connect these spaces through a rank-$k$ logical-signature map $M_{\rm log}:\mathbb F_2^q\to\mathbb F_2^k$. For fixed, error-independent orderings it yields the exact logical-signature distribution, the OSD-0 logical error rate, and the logical-class coverage of any fixed list. For minimum-cost list decoding we prove $P_L=P_{\rm miss}+P_{\rm sel}$, separating absent-class from wrong-selection failures. Hypergraph-product and bivariate-bicycle codes are consistent with the coverage predictions. On the $[\![144,12,12]\!]$ gross code, 672 coverage-aware candidates outperform 899 combination-sweep candidates (paired McNemar $p=0.013$), while two lists with identical logical coverage give $P_L=11.30\%$ and $3.78\%$; the signature-based coverage compression persists across 30 random column orderings. Logical coverage and within-class representative selection are therefore complementary resources that candidate count alone does not capture. The framework guides OSD list construction and compression by identifying coverage requirements and distinguishing coverage losses from failures of representative selection.

title: Exact Quantum Query Complexity of the Five-Bit Symmetric Boolean Function $\Exact^5_{3,4}$
authors: Guoliang Xu, Haoran Zhang, Mengfan Wu, Songyao Xue, Mingke Liu
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24518v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Let \(f = \text{EXACT}^5_{3,4}\) be the Boolean function that equals 1 exactly on inputs of Hamming weight 3 or 4. Earlier numerical studies reported success probabilities close to one using three queries, but the existence of an exact three-query algorithm had remained unresolved. This paper settles this problem by proving that the exact quantum query complexity of \(f\) is \(4\). For the lower bound, we express every three-query algorithm through layer-by-layer Gram matrices of low-degree Fourier coefficients. We then construct a fixed rational dual certificate whose slack matrices are all positive definite. This certificate separates the necessary Gram-matrix region from the exact-output condition and therefore rules out every exact algorithm using at most three queries in the stated model. The positivity verification reduces to five small rational matrices and Sylvester's criterion. For the upper bound, we invoke the previously known four-query algorithm for the seven-bit function \(\text{EXACT}^7_{3,4}\) and apply the standard padding reduction. To quantify the near-exact behavior, we use the same certificate to derive a valid, though not claimed tight, lower bound \(\frac{25600}{43779488192449}>0\) on the worst-case error of every algorithm using at most three queries. This positive error gap is compatible with the near-unit success probabilities reported in earlier numerical studies, which do not establish exact computation.

title: Ergotropy of nonequilibrium steady states beyond the full secular approximation
authors: Xing-Xing Hu, Hui-Yu Yang, Kun Zhang, Xiao-Hui Wang
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24561v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding the generation and activation of ergotropy, the maximum work extractable by cyclic unitary operations, is central to quantum battery research. Positive-temperature thermal states are passive, whereas nonequilibrium environments can sustain nonpassive steady states with nonzero ergotropy. However, the full secular approximation commonly used in Lindblad descriptions can suppress steady-state coherence and obscure its contribution to ergotropy. Using a Bloch-Redfield master equation beyond the full secular approximation, we investigate the ergotropy of the nonequilibrium steady state (NESS) of two exchange-coupled qubits connected to independent thermal reservoirs. The NESS ergotropy of two qubits with the same frequency is entirely coherent and grows quadratically with temperature bias near equilibrium. In contrast, detuned qubits can exhibit incoherent ergotropy. We derive an exact analytical criterion for its activation and show that activation requires the hotter reservoir to be coupled to the qubit with the higher bare frequency. Comparing NESSs obtained with and without full secularization reveals quantitative and qualitative differences in ergotropy that reflect changes in both its coherent and incoherent contributions. The results clarify the mechanisms of NESS ergotropy activation and demonstrate the importance of retaining steady-state coherence beyond the full secular approximation when characterizing stationary work resources.

title: Concatenated continuous-drive protection of exchange-based spin-qubit gates
authors: Takuma Kuno, Takeru Utsugi, Andrew J. Ramsay, Hideo Arimoto, Tetsuo Kodera, Hiroyuki Mizuno
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24582v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Exchange-based two-qubit gates in semiconductor spin qubits are sensitive to low-frequency detuning noise and control errors. Here, we extend concatenated continuous driving (CCD), implemented by phase modulation of a global microwave drive, to exchange-based SWAP and $\sqrt{\mathrm{SWAP}}$ operations between double-dressed spin qubits and investigate its effectiveness for protecting two-qubit gates. We find that CCD retains strong protection against quasistatic common-mode detuning errors while substantially improving robustness against Rabi-frequency errors and qubit-to-qubit Rabi-frequency mismatch compared with conventional continuous dressing. By contrast, the gate fidelity is impacted by differential detuning errors. By modeling partially correlated quasistatic detuning noise, we further show that the noise-averaged gate fidelity depends strongly on the spatial correlation of the qubit-frequency fluctuations, with positive correlations enhancing CCD protection by suppressing the differential-noise component. These results identify the symmetry and spatial correlation of qubit-frequency noise as key factors governing continuous-drive protection in coupled spin-qubit systems.

title: Autonomous Thermal Switching Outperforms the Frozen Optimum with Vanishing Correlations
authors: Siyi Deng, Longxing Xu, Zhuolin Ye, Xian He, Jianhui Wang
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24589v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Can autonomous thermal switching outperform the best frozen barrier allocation while keeping system--auxiliary correlations arbitrarily small? We establish this relaxation advantage at fixed lowering budget and visible equilibrium, preserving joint detailed balance. On finite reversible networks, optimal fast switching mixes profiles concentrating the budget on single edges. A three-state model gives a strict gain and its finite-rate threshold. Faster switching preserves the gain while correlations vanish throughout relaxation. Collective and continuous models suggest a colloidal test.

title: Fabric retrofit scenario analysis under uncertainty for an urban housing stock using machine learning
authors: Yunfei Bai, Aaron Tesfa Tsion, Ra\'ul Rosales, Barbara Shollock, Wei He
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24608v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fabric retrofit is central to decarbonising housing, and planning it depends on expected savings and their uncertainty. This study asks which upgrade saves most per dwelling and across a housing portfolio, how uncertain the savings are, and whether upgrade order matters. We propose an uncertainty-aware framework that converts predicted changes in energy performance certificate scores after wall, roof and window upgrades into standardised energy-cost savings and emission reductions. Six machine-learning models predict the 1-100 Standard Assessment Procedure (SAP) energy-cost and environmental impact (EI) emission scores from 17 certificate descriptors. Each model's errors on similar dwellings give calibrated prediction intervals. A global-best strategy applies the most accurate model throughout; a sample-specific strategy chooses each dwelling's model using these local errors. The analysis covers 103,414 officially registered dwellings in Westminster, London. CatBoost was the global-best model, with mean absolute errors of 3.487 SAP and 4.379 EI points on held-out dwellings. Both strategies projected similar savings; under global-best, roof insulation saved most per dwelling, GBP 203 annually (uncertainty range 176-229), and wall insulation most across the portfolio, GBP 6.09 million annually (uncertainty range 5.69-6.72). For 5,382 dwellings needing all three upgrades, every order delivered the same final package, yet installing roofs, walls, then windows a year apart accumulated 54% more projected cost savings over three years than the reverse order. Emission reductions followed the same pattern. Using only certificate data, the framework helps local authorities rank measures for dwellings and portfolios and sequence upgrades to bring savings forward.

title: SIESTA-QCOMP: Bridging Classical and Quantum Computing for Strongly Correlated Systems
authors: Yann Pouillon, Federico Marchesin, Ivano Tavernelli, Emilio Artacho
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24616v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Density Functional Theory (DFT) is the established workhorse of computational materials science, yet it faces fundamental challenges with strongly correlated electrons, such as in transition metal complexes and bond-breaking processes. While quantum computing offers a theoretically exact path to resolve these problems, current hardware limitations prohibit fully quantum simulations of realistic material systems. To bridge this gap, we present SIESTA-QCOMP, a modular suite embedding quantum methodologies within DFT. Harnessing SIESTA's localised basis set, we implement a projection-based embedding scheme that treats the bulk environment classically while mapping the strongly correlated "impurity" subspace to a quantum processor. The architecture uses a socket-based driver to orchestrate workflows between the Fortran-based SIESTA engine and Python-based frameworks like Qiskit, ensuring high interoperability. We detail the hybrid workflow, currently utilising a Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE), and discuss the road map toward methods such as Sample-based Quantum Diagonalisation (SQD). We illustrate the framework on an hypothetical iron porphyrin calculation and argue that such hybrid architectures are not merely interim solutions but essential foundations for integrating quantum utility into materials design, as envisioned by our broader QCOMP4DFT initiative.

title: Collective Strong Quantum Mpemba Effect in Accelerated Quantum Detectors
authors: G. D. de Moraes Neto, Richard Q. Matos, Norton G. de Almeida
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24658v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Collective coupling to the Minkowski vacuum allows uniformly accelerated quantum detectors to exhibit a strong quantum Mpemba effect, in which a state initially farther from equilibrium relaxes faster than a closer one. We establish the existence of this effect for every fixed finite number of detectors $N\geq 2$ at sufficiently small transverse separation within the pointlike secular master equation. The mechanism originates from two reflection sectors whose populations are conserved by the leading collective dynamics. Weak intersector transfer at finite separation generates an isolated, parametrically slow relaxation mode. A simple family of initial states permits its leading-order cancellation by matching the equilibrium sector populations, while a corrected preparation eliminates the slow-mode amplitude exactly. We construct a reference state that establishes a genuine reversal of trace-distance ordering. Numerical calculations and local-rate-preserving controls identify the collective origin of the effect, while spatially smeared detector calculations support its persistence within the second-order secular framework. The same mechanism extends to detectors coupled to a common thermal field, with analytically distinct slow relaxation rates. Thus, strong Mpemba relaxation is not exclusive to acceleration but emerges from a more general interplay between collective dissipation, reflection-sector conservation, and weak symmetry-breaking transfer.

title: Spontaneous particle-hole symmetry breaking in a disordered two-site quantum breakdown model
authors: Kinya Guan
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24669v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study spontaneous particle-hole symmetry breaking in a disordered two-site quantum breakdown model. The model is solvable in the limit of a large number of fermionic modes on each site. For a small ratio of the numbers of modes on the two sites, we derive the free energy analytically and find a finite-temperature symmetry-breaking transition. This transition changes from continuous to first order as the number of fermions produced in each conversion increases. Numerical results show that both types of transition persist beyond this regime, with an order-parameter exponent close to $1/2$ for continuous transitions.

title: Efficient Quantum Algorithm for Mixed-State Quantum Geometry
authors: Chenyang Wang, Qi Zhao, Xiao Yuan, Xiaoxia Cai
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24686v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mixed-state quantum geometry plays a fundamental role in quantum metrology, multiparameter estimation, and the characterization of quantum many-body systems. Yet, unlike its pure-state counterpart, accessing mixed-state geometry requires solving an ill-conditioned Lyapunov equation for the symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD), posing a major challenge for resource-efficient quantum computation. Here we address the challenge and develop a novel quantum algorithmic framework for efficiently accessing the quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM) and quantum geometric tensor (QGT) of mixed states. Our key insight is to uncover a previously unexplored connection between the positive semidefinite structure of density matrices and exponentially convergent Gauss-Laguerre quadrature, enabling an efficient integral-based construction of the SLD. A rigorous complexity analysis further establishes the resource efficiency of our algorithm, demonstrating logarithmic precision dependence and double-logarithmic ancillary-qubit overhead at fixed conditioning. Building on this construction, we achieve near-Heisenberg precision scaling for diagonal QFI estimation without quantum phase estimation and construct unified block encodings of the full QFIM and QGT under a bounded spectral-gap assumption. A complementary regularized algorithm extends efficient diagonal estimation to exponentially small spectral gaps under a bounded-response condition. Our results establish a resource-efficient route to coherent mixed-state quantum geometry, enabling its direct integration into quantum linear-algebra algorithms without classical reconstruction and opening new possibilities for quantum-enhanced multiparameter metrology.

title: Charge-Selective Displacement of Spatiotemporal Optical Vortices at a Spatially Uniform Time Boundary
authors: Chao Mei, Peilong Yang
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24713v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: At a spatially uniform, in-plane-isotropic time boundary, the transverse displacement of a spatiotemporal optical vortex changes sign with its topological charge, despite a charge-independent conversion weight. Radial spectral filtering couples to the vortex phase while preserving identical converted spectral intensities for opposite charges. For a narrow scalar Gaussian spectrum, the displacement follows the logarithmic slope of the spectral weight and occurs with zero mean transverse momentum. In a finite pumped GaAs waveguide, unequal attenuation during extraction adds angular deflection. Independent Maxwell--Drude simulations test this extraction-induced response and give $\pm42$~mrad before detector filtering. Calculated centroid traces at multiple planes separate propagation-induced drift from position offsets.

title: Realization of valley-controlled orbital angular momentum via inter-orbital coupling
authors: Wenxia Xu, Ziteng Wang, Yihan Wang, Qinggang Shang, Liqin Tang, Jingjun Xu, Hrvoje Buljan, Daohong Song, Zhigang Chen
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24714v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Orbital angular momentum (OAM) represents a fundamental degree of freedom (DoF) for understanding novel phenomena in solids and synthetic lattices. However, the generation and control of OAM in lattice systems remain challenging. Here, we experimentally observe valley-controlled OAM states in inversion-symmetry-broken photonic honeycomb lattices consisting of s- and higher-orbital sublattices. These OAM states manifest as chiral vortex arrays in real space. By selectively exciting s-orbital modes carrying no initial OAM at either the K or K' valley, we observe higher-orbital OAM modes generated via inter-orbital coupling in neighboring sites. Specifically, s-p orbital coupling generates OAM states with topological charge l=+1 or l=-1, while s-d orbital coupling yields higher-charge OAM states with l=+2 or l=-2. The sign of the topological charge is determined by the valley DoF, enabling deterministic control of vortex chirality across the entire array. Our theory further reveals that a local vortex-chirality symmetry enforces the valley-dependent selection of vortex chirality at the K and K' valleys, establishing a direct connection between the valley DoF and real-space vortex chirality. These results establish a versatile platform for engineering chiral vortex arrays via orbital physics and exploring orbital- and topology-mediated phenomena in photonic systems and beyond.

title: Boosting fluorescence and polarization with nanophotonics for single-molecule chiral sensing
authors: Ershad Mohammadi, T. V. Raziman, Alberto G. Curto
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24746v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Detecting chirality is essential in chemistry and biomedicine. Circular dichroism identifies chiral molecules through their differential absorption of circularly polarized light. However, its sensitivity is limited by vanishing absorption at low concentrations. Fluorescence-based methods have already enabled other optical techniques to reach the single-molecule limit and could, in principle, also extend chiral detection to reach this sensitivity regime. They are marred, however, by the combination of weak fluorescence signals and low polarization contrast. To overcome these limitations, we leverage high-index dielectric nanophotonics to simultaneously enhance both fluorescence and polarization for chiral sensing. We propose a reciprocity-based analytical framework for a chiral dipolar emitter coupled to a nanoantenna and reveal the different contributions and trade-offs governing the enhancement of circularly polarized fluorescence. Guided by this insight, we tailor achiral dielectric nanostructures to reach a 1000-fold enhancement of fluorescence intensity together with a 10-fold increase in polarization. Crucially, we show that accounting for extrinsic polarization effects in the angular emission patterns of nanophotonic structures is indispensable for reliable enantiomer discrimination. Our approach opens a realistic path for single-molecule chiral sensing.

title: Adiabatic controlled-$Z$ gate for neutral atoms with F\"orster-enhanced Rydberg dressing
authors: Diksha Thapliyal, Ajay Wasan
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24755v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study an adiabatic controlled-$Z$ (CZ) gate for neutral atoms in which dipole-dipole coupling between nearly degenerate Rydberg pair states enhances the interaction between dressed ground states. This coupling produces an avoided crossing in the two-atom dressed-state spectrum. Approaching the crossing enhances the dressed interaction, but also reduces the dressed-state gap and increases the Rydberg admixture. We identify a F\"orster-enhanced operating range in which the required conditional phase is accumulated with adiabatic return and small transient Rydberg population. We then analyze the finite-time dynamics of the two-qubit computational states under a smooth pulse. Reducing the dressing strength weakens the dressed interaction, so maintaining the target phase at the same pulse duration requires operation closer to the avoided crossing, where the Rydberg admixture increases. This dependence is then used to select the shortest gate at a fixed peak Rabi frequency in the F\"orster-enhanced operating range that accumulates the CZ phase with high Bell-state fidelity while keeping the Rydberg population small. Changing the F\"orster defect shifts the avoided crossing, while the gate parameters change only weakly. For a specific rubidium F\"orster channel, the selected gate corresponds to experimentally relevant laser coupling, pulse duration, and interatomic separation. We also estimate errors from the finite Rydberg lifetime and from weak excitation of a neighboring spectator atom. For the parameters considered, the spectator-induced error remains below the finite-lifetime contribution.

title: Strategic Origins of Network Structure
authors: Christoph Riedl, Rory Smead
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24792v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The structure and dynamics of complex networks are intimately linked. Despite immense progress in statistically characterizing these systems, a generalized mechanistic framework explaining why specific mesoscale structures emerge remains elusive. Here we introduce the game-graph equilibrium, the stable rest point of a payoff-driven partner-choice dynamic, analogous to a Nash equilibrium. This reveals network structure as the fossilized record of strategic interaction. We prove analytically that two-type games have exactly four network topologies, which are their exhaustive thermodynamic phases: assortative, disassortative, and two core-peripheries. This result generalizes to $K^K$ topological classes for $K$-type interactions. Furthermore, four distinct Nash equilibria produce core-periphery topologies, yet their payoffs reveal whether the underlying dynamic is cooperative or exploitative. To recover the generating dynamics from observed networks, we develop mechanistic inference by constraining a block model to lie on a low-dimensional, game-theoretic manifold. Applied to real-world networks, the model yields interpretable quantities, distinguishes states that look identical to conventional methods, predicts network topologies it has never seen without retraining, and controls its own complexity without hand-tuned penalties. Networks such as international trade are well described by the model despite the hard constraint, suggesting that real-world systems are organized by payoff-driven partner choice. Our framework resolves a foundational ambiguity by offering a precise, mechanistic definition of communities: strategic equivalence.

title: Modeling the Coevolution of Human Skills and AI Adoption
authors: Giacomo Frigerio, Susanna Caruso, Giacomo Livan, Vito Latora
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24794v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The value of relying on generative AI depends on two quantities that evolve with its use: users' unaided skill, which may decline without practice, and the originality of AI-assisted work, which may decline as more people rely on similar tools. We model this process as a coevolutionary game in which individuals choose between autonomous and AI-assisted work, with autonomous practice strengthening their skills while reliance on AI gradually erodes them. When the reinforcing effect of skill erosion outweighs the crowding cost of lost originality, the population exhibits two alternative stable states: low AI adoption with high average skill, and high AI adoption with low average skill. Because skill is individual, autonomous workers remain more skilled than AI users, making autonomous work less vulnerable to population-wide skill decline. The strength of this effect is governed by a timescale ratio: the rate at which skills adapt relative to the rate at which individuals change strategy. The same ratio determines the full distribution of skills, which we derive analytically. Populations with identical AI adoption and average skill can differ sharply: when strategies change frequently, skills remain homogeneous and collective lock-in to high AI adoption is stronger; when strategies persist, lock-in weakens but the population can polarize into highly skilled autonomous workers and AI-dependent individuals. Modeling output overlap further shows that more diverse AI outputs can make widespread adoption harder to reverse. Together, these results expose tradeoffs between the benefits of widespread AI adoption and its long-run risks, making collective lock-in and skill polarization distinct intervention targets.

title: An Accurate Zeroth-Order Perturbation Theory for Solving Power-Law Potentials within the Framework of the Asymptotic Iteration Method
authors: A. J. Sous, Ibsal Assi, Nasser Saad
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24805v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spherically symmetric singular potentials have a wide range of applications, such as molecular and atomic physics. In this work, we present a zeroth-order perturbation theory for solving the Schr\"odinger equation within the framework of the asymptotic iteration method (AIM). We rely on exponential and hyperbolic potential ansatz substitutions, where the difference between the original and new potential is treated as a small perturbation. Each potential ansatz has a free parameter chosen small enough to give an accurate zeroth-order perturbative wave equation solution. This method avoids the oscillatory behavior observed in the asymptotic iteration solutions when applying the AIM to such problems. Finally, we illustrate our approach by solving a few problems, particularly potentials with quartic and sextic singularities. We compare our results with those obtained via other methods and find good agreement.

title: Characterizing Local and Correlated Pauli Noise in Quantum Teleportation Circuits
authors: L. Anjos, Jose Alfredo de Leon, R. S. Sarthour, Alejandro Fonseca
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24840v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We analytically characterize how the location and the local or correlated structure of stochastic Pauli errors affect a three-qubit coherent quantum-teleportation circuit. Independent local channels and a fully correlated two-qubit channel are inserted separately in six configurations. Propagating each Pauli-error realization through the Clifford circuit yields the effective channel on Bob's qubit and analytical expressions for the average and state-resolved fidelities. Under a common ordered-pair probability convention, the six configurations form three pairs that induce equivalent reduced channels on Bob. Within each pair, corresponding Pauli-error realizations have the same probabilities and produce the same effective Pauli operator on Bob's output state. The equivalence therefore holds for every input state within the stochastic Pauli models considered here, rather than only for the average fidelity. Correlated Z errors do not affect the output for the first pair; local X and Z errors exhibit complementary qubit sensitivity for the second; and correlated same-axis Pauli errors cancel for the third. These results classify the error response of the selected circuit configurations and show that it depends jointly on the error statistics, Pauli axis, and position within the protocol.

title: Where should we look for the deviation from quantum mechanics?
authors: Jerome Nicolas, Albert Schwarz
abstract:
arXiv:2610.24857v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We argue that the experimental measurement of the lifetime and decay law of metastable helium is a promising way to find a deviation from quantum mechanics. We analyze the decay of the metastable state for a quartic deformation of quantum mechanics. We find that the absolute change of the mean lifetime can be significant even if the modification is small. We show that, in the Wigner--Weisskopf approximation, the deviation from the exponential law in the modified theory can occur on time scales comparable with the lifetime.
